title: Evaluating Budgeting Apps: Limited Support for Budgeting Compared to Tracking
tldr: A functionality review of 45 top-rated budgeting apps reveals that one third lack budgeting support beyond tracking, with inconsistent terminology and poor grounding in mental accounting theory.
problem_and_motivation: Despite the rapid growth of budgeting apps, limited HCI research has evaluated their functionalities through a theoretical lens. Mental accounting theory offers a framework for understanding how people organize and track spending, yet existing apps show insufficient support for budgeting informed by money envelopes.
approach: Searched Google Play Store and Apple Store using keywords budget, budgeting, and finance, identifying 1335 apps.
Filtered to 45 top-rated free apps with at least 1000 reviews and 4+ rating through iterative exclusion.
Conducted expert evaluation of all 45 apps on Galaxy S21+ and five apps on iPhone 12.
Applied mental accounting theory concepts to identify functionalities related to funds, expenditures, categories, and money envelopes.
Used iterative discussion between two authors over several months to reconcile identified functionalities.
findings: num: All 45 apps support expense tracking, but only 26 support multiple budget categories.
num: 35 apps support transfer transactions between accounts, allowing money movement from income to expense or saving.
num: 19 apps rely on single budget for all expenses rather than category-specific money envelopes.
num: Only 7 apps integrate with online banking for automatic transaction import.
num: Only 2 apps explicitly mention design informed by money envelope systems.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: PRISMA diagram of app selection process from 1335 to 45 apps → Systematic filtering identified top-rated budgeting apps.
Table 1: Functionalities of funds and expenses across 45 apps → All apps support expense creation, most support income creation, currency and date entry.
Table 2: Transaction accounts, transfers, and budget monitoring across 45 apps → 26 apps support multiple budgets, 35 support transfers between accounts.

topics.justification: Discusses limitations of category systems including subcategories, one-off categories, and alignment with mental accounting theory.

topics.name: Landscape of Existing Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Comprehensive review of 45 top-rated budgeting apps across Google Play and Apple Store.

topics.name: Limitations and Gaps in Existing Systems

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides the first systematic functionality review of budgeting apps through the lens of mental accounting theory.
directly_justifies: One third of the 45 top-rated budgeting apps do not support budgeting informed by money envelopes.
Only 26 of 45 apps support multiple budgets aligned with mental accounting theory.
Most apps use banking domain terminology for accounts rather than clear mental accounting categories.
Only 7 apps integrate with online banking for automatic transaction import.
All 45 apps support expense tracking but only 35 support transfer transactions between accounts.
limits: Study limited to UK marketplaces (Google Play and Apple Store) with English-language apps.
Expert evaluation conducted on a single device per platform rather than comprehensive testing.
No user study to validate findings about real user behavior with the apps.
Methodology relies on expert evaluation rather than systematic feature comparison against a theoretical framework.
No analysis of app pricing models or premium feature limitations.

limitations: Study limited to UK marketplace apps, limiting generalizability to other markets.
Expert evaluation rather than user study, potentially missing real usability issues.
No quantitative analysis of app feature completeness against mental accounting theory.
Premium features excluded from analysis may represent significant functionality gaps.
The paper does not evaluate actual user effectiveness of the reviewed apps.
remember_this: All 45 top-rated budgeting apps support expense tracking, but only 26 support multiple budget categories.
One third of apps rely on single budgets rather than money envelopes for different expense categories.
Apps use inconsistent terminology for accounts, drawing from both banking and everyday financial practices.
Only 2 apps explicitly mention design informed by money envelope systems.
Four design implications proposed for clearer terminology and better budgeting support.
